article.title: Google Cloud Makes Self-Managed VMware Cloud Foundation Generally Available on Z3 Bare Metal in 22 Regions, With a Terraform Deployment Path
article.summary: Google Cloud's VMware solution runs VCF 9.x on Z3 bare metal in 22 regions with bring-your-own licenses; Google's own pages differ on managed-service licensing and machine types.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Google Cloud has made its self-managed VMware offering, VMware solution on Google Cloud, generally available. It runs VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.x on dedicated Compute Engine bare-metal instances, and Google's [launch post](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/infrastructure-modernization/vmware-solution-on-google-cloud/) describes it as "giving you full administrative authority for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated Google Cloud bare metal." Google's [release notes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/release-notes) date general availability to October 27, 2026, and the launch post is dated October 28, 2026; neither states a time zone. The trade publication [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/11/google-cloud-self-managed-vmware/) reported the launch on November 8, 2026.

## What Google Announced

The new option sits beside Google Cloud VMware Engine, the Google-managed service. According to the [launch post](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/infrastructure-modernization/vmware-solution-on-google-cloud/), VMware Engine runs VCF 5.2 on ve1 and ve2 node families, offers role-based vCenter administrative privileges, and has patching, updates and monitoring managed by Google. The new offering runs VCF 9.x on Compute Engine bare metal, gives full root administrative access across ESXi, vCenter, NSX Manager and the rest of the VCF components, and leaves updates to the customer or a partner using VCF Operations tools.

Each node is a z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal instance, which Google's post describes as 4th Generation Intel Xeon with 96 physical cores (192 hyper-threads), 1.5 TB of RAM, 72 TB of all-flash NVMe storage and 200 Gbps networking. Storage is VMware vSAN on the local NVMe drives, and the post says NetApp volumes are also supported. The post puts availability at 22 Google Cloud regions, with more planned in upcoming quarters.

The post carries three figures that are Google's own claims: NVMe memory tiering "can reduce server TCO by up to 40%", vSAN Express Storage Architecture "reduces storage TCO by up to 39% compared to traditional external arrays", and "Up to 80% live patching coverage for critical security updates". The only customer quoted in the post is Scott Ronan, Senior Director of Platforms, Databases & Cloud at GXO Logistics, who says "Our early assessment shows significant potential."

## What Provisioning Involves

Google's documentation, as read on November 9, 2026, offers two routes. According to the [deployment options page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/deployment-options), deployment can use a guided workflow in the Google Cloud console or Infrastructure as Code templates with Terraform. The same page lists the Terraform route as best for "Repeatable production deployments, automated CI/CD pipelines, and version-controlled infrastructure".

The [Terraform guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/deploy-terraform) requires Terraform CLI version 1.3.0 or later and says the identity running Terraform, "a human administrator or an automated CI/CD service account", needs the Compute Admin, DNS Administrator and Service Account User roles. The automation provisions the ESXi bare-metal hosts, Layer 2 broadcast networks with an MTU of 8896, Cloud DNS private zones and regional internal load balancers.

The [deployment options page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/deployment-options) says the project must be enabled for VLAN-based networking, a step that involves a support ticket asking for Layer 2 connectivity to be allowlisted, and that the console's self-managed option is not visible until the project is enabled. The [quotas page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/quotas) says the deployment consumes Compute Engine quotas rather than VMware Engine API node quotas, that a standard high-availability vSphere cluster requires a minimum of four bare-metal nodes, and that quotas "don't guarantee hardware capacity availability in a region or zone."

The [known issues page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/known-issues) lists several that affect automation, among them the following. Google Cloud VPC networks support an MTU of up to 8896 bytes, while VCF by default configures distributed switches, VMkernel adapters and NSX transport node profiles with 9000, and oversized frames are dropped. Because the VPC enforces strict source and destination IP checks on each node's Dynamic NICs, the vMotion and vSAN addresses VCF assigns to a host must match those on the corresponding Compute Engine Dynamic NIC; the page says the toolkit sorts the hostSpecs and includeIpAddressRanges arrays in the deployment file to handle this. The page also says the default NSX virtual switch mode in VCF 9.x, Enhanced Datapath Standard, is not supported on these hosts.

## Where the Sources Differ

Three points in the sources do not line up, and the pages cited here do not explain them.

- **Licensing for the managed service.** The launch post's comparison table lists "Bring Your Own License (BYOL) portable VCF subscriptions" for VMware Engine as well as for the new offering. Google's [compare-models page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-solution/compare-models) says of the managed service: "VMware software licenses are included with the service."
- **Machine types.** The launch post and release notes name z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal. The Terraform guide lists "z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal or z3-highmem-192-metal".
- **The 39% figure.** InfoQ describes the 40% and 39% TCO figures as "presented without a baseline or methodology". Google's post attaches "compared to traditional external arrays" to the 39% figure and names no comparison for the 40% figure, and it states no methodology for either.

InfoQ also reports that the announcement "gives no pricing, no SLA, no list of the 22 regions, and names no migration path from VMware Engine’s VCF 5.2 to the self-managed 9.x stack." None of the Google pages cited in this article contains a price, an SLA, a list of the 22 regions or such a migration path; the Herald did not search other Google pages.

## How It Compares

InfoQ says Google joins Oracle and AWS in offering customer-operated VCF on bare metal, while Azure VMware Solution remains a Microsoft-operated service. AWS's [July 6, 2026 blog post](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/migration-and-modernization/vmware-cloud-foundation-vcf-9-0-and-9-1-on-amazon-evs/) says VCF 9.0 and 9.1 are available on Amazon Elastic VMware Service "giving you complete control over your VCF installation", with EC2 metal instances running ESX 9.x in the customer's VPC. Microsoft's [product page](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/azure-vmware/) offers Azure VMware Solution as "a fully managed service" with patches and upgrades from Microsoft.

InfoQ frames the choice as a trade: the managed model lets the provider absorb Broadcom's release cadence and licensing changes, while the self-managed model hands both back in exchange for root access and the current VCF major version. It quotes the consultancy Xtravirt, which it identifies as one of the launch partners, saying full control "is only worth having if someone in your organisation wants that responsibility." Google's post names Xtravirt among its fifteen partners (the Herald's count of the list), and InfoQ reports that Accenture, HCL, IBM, Infosys, TCS and Wipro are among the partners offering managed operations on top of the customer-owned stack.

The Herald [previously reported](/article/2026-07/16-botched-network-update-triggers-12-hour-google-cloud-vmware-engine-outage-across-three-regions) a July 14, 2026 incident that disrupted Google Cloud VMware Engine stretched-cluster environments in Sydney, Melbourne and Frankfurt; that concerned the Google-managed service, not the offering described here.
